                        <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 id="Abs1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number"> </span>Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>Synthetic genomics (SynGen) has emerged as a new game-changing platform for future crop improvement by allowing the design and construction of designer-made plant genomes for sustainable agriculture. This chapter first discussed the conceptual and technological foundations of SynGen for future genome design. We investigated how SynGen is being applied to improve yield, stress tolerance, nutritional profile, metabolic pathway engineering, plant–microbe interactions, and to design minimal or fully synthetic plant genomes. Integration with multi-omics, biofoundries, and gene drives further expands its capability to fast-track future crop design. Nevertheless, widespread application encounters major technical, ethical, and regulatory challenges, along with some bottlenecks and implications of redesigned crops, which demand transparent governance and inclusive public dialogue. To address these issues, we propose that innovations in synthetic biology and public–private collaborations could assist in the design of future climate-smart, high-performance crops. In short, SynGen could serve as a game-changing approach that can help achieve global food security in the face of changing climate.</p></div></div></section>

        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showthanksmessage') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = "block";
            mainPanel.style.display = "none";
            thankYouMessageAuthenticated.innerHTML = "Thank you for subscribing to the " + displaySubscriptionType + " for " + journalTitle + ".";

            displaySubscriptionType = subscriptionType;
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showthanksmessage') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = "block";
            mainPanel.style.display = "none";
            thankYouMessageAuthenticated.innerHTML = "Thank you for subscribing to the " + displaySubscriptionType + " for " + journalTitle + ".";

    </ul></section><div class="ejp-fulltext-content js-ejp-fulltext-content"><section id="ArticleBody"><p id="JCL-P-0">I am honored and thrilled to have the privilege of giving this presentation. This really is the culmination of my academic career and I cannot be more grateful. Thank you to President Dan Hoh and the CNS Executive Committee for granting me this honor. I feel truly blessed to be here and am enthusiastic about supporting Dan's theme for the meeting. It is impossible to begin this presentation without thanking and acknowledging those who have provided me the opportunities which led up to this moment. I would first like to acknowledge my mentors during residency at the University of Pittsburgh. Peter Jannetta, Dade Lunsford, and Doug Kondziolka, all three past honored guests of this society (no pressure by the way), were the leadership team who created an environment of inquiry, ambition, competition, and collaboration which functioned as a crucible for the training of outstanding neurosurgeons. The resident team at that time now reads like a who's who of academic medicine and I was forced to up my game to keep up with the crowd. I need to acknowledge Ed Benzel, another CNS Honored Guest who has taught all of us so much about spinal biomechanics but more importantly has taught us about balancing academic and professional success with compassion and common sense. Ed is truly the definition of a mentor- he provides insight, knowledge, and support without judgement. He is available when sought out but does not insert himself into life decisions. Thank you Ed for your wisdom over the years and for your kind introduction this morning. I need to give a special shout out to Mark Hadley. Mark, as all of you know, injects energy into any project that he is part of. Mark took over a spine section initiative to develop a set of evidence-based guidelines for the management of cervical spine injuries in the late 1990's/early 2000's. He somehow managed to twist Beverly Walters's arm into joining the effort as a mentor and McMaster's methodology guru and recruited a committee to get the job done. I had volunteered for the committee several years beforehand but had not been invited to participate. Somehow, Mark thought I might be a good fit and I was invited to join an all-star committee: three future CNS Presidents, two future NASS Presidents, a future editor of <em xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Neurosurgery</em>, and three current or future section chairs. Mark gave me my assignments and just as in residency, I had to up my game to keep up. That project was a game changer for my career. It led to my appointment to lead the lumbar fusion guidelines and an appointment on the CNS Executive Committee and set me on the course which led here. Thank you, Mark. Finally, I will only briefly mention my debt to Bob Dempsey and Greg Trost here as I will elaborate more in a few minutes. Bob has created an incredible environment at the University of Wisconsin and has done such outstanding work “clearing the field” for his faculty and residents. For the past 30 years he has worked to remove obstacles to success for all of us and has enabled many of us to thrive both within and outside of the department. Greg has been my “partner in spine” since 1998. We met on a hill outside of Albuquerque and have been joined at the hip since. He has been an unbelievably supportive mentor, partner, and friend. He has wisdom that at some point was beyond his years, however at this point he has grown into it! Thank you Bob and Greg.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-1">I struggled making this talk. I generally do much better when I am assigned a project on a particular topic. My background is in literature synthesis, so I really enjoy searching the literature and doing an analysis and trying to reach reasonable conclusions about which treatment strategy is superior to others and give a nod to the strength of those conclusions. The theme of this meeting is “Connections in Neurosurgery.” My initial thought for this project was to explore the role of community and connections in improving the neurosurgical experience from a variety of perspectives- patient, physician, and society. My hypothesis was that the presence of a supportive “community” and the availability of “connections” would help prevent burnout and in turn improve patient care. I did a literature search which revealed a fairly robust discussion of burnout in neurosurgery and a philosophical framework regarding an unexplored link to the role of “humanism” in both influencing the doctor patient relationship and in providing a sense of community and value to the physician. I imagined presenting an evidence-based discussion of the value of community and humanism in neurosurgery. My plan was to first define humanism, present the evidence for its value in modern medicine and neurosurgery, and then wrap up with a cogent plan to actively incorporate its principles into everyday practice.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-2">I began to dig deeper into the concept of humanism and discovered Emmanuel Levinas. Levinas was a Lithuanian born Jew who grew up during the years of World War I and the Russian Revolution. This led to some instability and a temporary move to Kharkiv in Ukraine as a child/early teenager. His early education was secular but on return from Ukraine he attended a Jewish school for several years before emigrating to France. He studied in Strasbourg and then the University of Freiburg where he began his studies on phenomenology. He became a French citizen in 1939 and reported for military duty in 1940. His unit was surrounded during the German invasion and he spent the rest of the war as a prisoner of war.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R1">1</a></sup></sup> His philosophy was deeply effected by these life experiences and he wrote extensively about the concept of the “other.” My incomplete, naïve, and overly simplistic concept of Levinas' “other” was formed through painfully working my way through two texts, <em xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Humanism of the Other</em>, a translation of Levinas' own writings and <em xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Origins of the Other</em>, a discussion of his philosophy by Samuel Moyn.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R2 R3">2,3</a></sup></sup> I was continually amazed by the fact that I could know the meaning of every word in a paragraph yet have no idea what the paragraph meant without rereading it repeatedly. My cliff-note interpretation of the “other” is that this represents a spark of the divine in each of us and that to be human it is critical that we care for this spark in others. Clearly one can see the difficulty Levinas must have had reconciling this philosophy with the dehumanizing behaviors of the Nazis during WWII and the multitude of atrocities committed since. As I worked my way down into the rabbit hole of Judeo-French-Phenomenology, I realized that turning this into a talk with any relevance to modern neurosurgery was going to be a struggle.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-3">It was at this point that I had three conversations which changed the direction of my talk. The first was with Darius Ansari, one of our fourth-year residents. Darius won one of the Charlie Kuntz awards at the Spine Section meeting this past year and he and I spent some time together at the meeting. One of the most fun parts of the spine section meeting is the Cahill Debates. These debates usually pit folks who are known to have divergent opinions in a spirited debate with the audience voting on who wins the argument after both presenters have spoken. When I have been invited to participate, I have uniformly been assigned the less sexy, the less expensive, and the less new option to defend. There are no rules, and personal attacks are not only allowed, but are encouraged. I have always prepared for these debates with an extensive literature search, an exhaustive analysis of the literature, and a cogent and well supported conclusion to make my point. I get slaughtered all the time. After losing a debate regarding a ridiculously expensive, poorly conceived, and completely useless new technology to Dan Riew, who presented no facts but did create a very amusing Jib Jab video of me as a dinosaur, I complained to Darius over drinks that evening and he counseled me as follows: Dr Resnick, you need to stop bringing facts to a powerpoint fight.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-4">The second conversation was with Asdrubal Falavigna, a Brazilian neurosurgeon and decades old friend. Asdrubal had invited me to participate as a speaker in the Brazilian Neurosurgical Congress. As many of you know, it is an honor to participate in these events, and the hosts spend a lot of money to get you there. In return for this investment, one is often assigned multiple presentations. I had six or seven presentations to give over a two-day period. Some of these were canned talks that I had given before and were quite dry and evidence based-topics such as comparing long-term outcomes of cervical arthroplasty vs cervical fusion (spoiler alert- there's no difference). Other talks, such as a talk about a terrible complication that I had caused weeks before the meeting, were less scripted and more anecdotal. Once I completed my tenure at the meeting, Asdrubal took me out to lunch on the way back to the airport. As we were reflecting over the last few days Asdrubal said to me, “Dan, when you present it is better if you just talk.” He meant to say that I should lighten up on my use of “<em xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">twenty-seven 8 by 10 color glossy photographs with circles and arrows and a paragraph on the back of each one to be used as evidence in court</em>,<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R4">4</a></sup></sup>” and focus more on the underlying truths behind contemporary practice.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-5">The third conversation was with Jake Bethel, our other fourth year resident. This conversation occurred over a lumbar fusion. Everything was going fine and we were chatting about several things. One item was me lamenting my difficulty in putting this talk together. Jake was asking me some questions about fellowships and the job market. I expressed my deep concern about changes in the economic landscape of neurosurgery and in particular the hazards faced by recent graduates of our residency programs. As I went on and on through irrigation, drain placement, and fascial closure, Jake said: “Dr Resnick, you should talk about that stuff!” So that is what I decided to do. The remainder of this presentation is going to be an evidence-informed discussion of real-world problems that I have seen first and second hand through my experiences as a practicing neurosurgeon, a program director, and as one with a long history of involvement with organized neurosurgery, in particular the American Board of Neurological Surgeons.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-6">I believe that our specialty of neurosurgery is facing an existential threat. I acknowledge that there are many broader threats to our survival and society- festering wars in Ukraine and Gaza, continued unrest through sub-Saharan Africa; fractured political systems here in the United States as well as abroad, Brazil for example, where people who live in the same towns and salute the same flag cannot even treat each other with common decency let alone make productive decisions to better the plight of their citizens; and continued threats of widespread conflagration with biological and nuclear weapons to name a few. Today I am going to focus on a phenomenon that while not entirely unique to neurosurgery, disproportionately effects our graduates compared with any other group. Allow me to set the stage.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-7">When I was finishing residency, most of the available jobs were in private practice with a substantial minority in academics and a smattering of jobs in alternative models (military, locums, and Kaiser for example). In traditional private practice and in academics, junior neurosurgeons answer to senior neurosurgeons in the same practice. The senior neurosurgeons have an inherent investment in the junior partner and a shared goal for the junior partner's success. Mentorship is an inherent part of the business relationship and the better the mentorship, the better the practice/department does as a whole. I'd like to provide two quick examples of how early mentorship helped me out immensely early in my career. The first story relates to my partner Greg Trost. My first elective case as an attending was a microdiskectomy on a very nice middle-aged Italian man who owned a business in town. I did the microdiskectomy with the chief resident at the time, and I thought we did a pretty good job. Unfortunately, my patient did not get better at all. I repeated the MRI which was not perfect but was pretty good. I saw him back three or four times and was really feeling insecure about my surgical skills. I presented the case to Greg, and he paused for about three seconds before saying “You know Dan, they don't all always get better.” Those 10 seconds of interaction allowed me to shed pounds of weight and allowed me to forgive myself for not being perfect. The ability to recognize that I can't make everyone better and that it is not necessarily a defect in my performance in every case has been invaluable to me throughout my career. I have not in fact, been able to make everyone better. The second anecdote involves my Chairman, Bob Dempsey. Early in my tenure at University of Wisconsin I had a patient come in with an urgent but not emergent problem. I can't remember the exact circumstances, but it was a case that had to get done today but not necessarily RIGHT NOW. I finished rounding around 7 <span style="font-variant: small-caps;" xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">am</span> and went to the operating room control desk to see if I could get a room to get the case done. As it turned out (unbelievable in today's packed operating rooms), there was an open neurosurgery room. My partner Benny Iskandar had a shunt scheduled later that day (after clinic) and they were holding the room for him. Wonderful! I exclaimed, I can get my case in and out and Benny will never be the wiser. The OR staff refused however, mainly because they did not feel like tearing down and resetting up the room. I found this absurd and essentially politely refused to leave the control desk until my patient was on their way to the operating room. Well, this pissed some middle managers off and a few days later I was called to Bob's office after a complaint. Bob asked me what happened, I explained the situation, and after a few seconds he said “Well, I would have done the same thing.” Knowing that my chairman had my back gave me the confidence that as long as I was trying to do the right thing, I would be supported. These two interactions, neither one taking more than a minute had a significant impact on how I carried myself and how I viewed my role at the University Hospital.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-8">Today, the job situation is very different. Although about 30% of jobs remain in academics, the majority of nonacademic jobs are now hospital employed positions. Making the matter worse, many academic programs, such as my own, are now run through hospital owned corporations. True private practice opportunities are few and far between. Now, I am not saying that everything has always been hunky dory in private practice, there have always been the occasional scoundrels who game the system at the expense of others. That said however, in traditional academic and private practice, pay, advancement and strategic planning initiatives are in the hands of senior neurosurgeons who know the job intimately. That is simply not true today where such decisions lie in the hands of healthcare administrators, few of whom have ever seen the hospital at night let alone understand what the demands of a neurosurgical practice are. What happened to the private practice sector in neurosurgery?</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-9">In short, the private practice sector has been systematically eliminated by payment and policy decisions implemented by both parties. The most obvious example is the continuous decline in reimbursement we have seen over the last 25 years or more. When I finished training, a private practice could support itself almost exclusively on professional charges. Neurosurgeons would form independent businesses and then contract with community hospitals for privileges. Community hospitals, eager for the contribution margin associated with neurosurgical procedures and in need of emergency call support, would actively recruit the neurosurgical practices through incentives such as top-of-the-line equipment, call stipends, administrative support, and guaranteed access to facilities. Reimbursement was such that a neurosurgeon operating two to three days a week could make a very nice living without reliance on subsidies. Many practices would invest in imaging centers, physical therapy services, or real estate to supplement their income. What has happened? To start with, reimbursement has dropped substantially. Despite years of lobbying, thousands of visits to Capitol Hill, and multiple consortiums physicians as a whole and neurosurgeons in particular have been penalized by both parties. Between the years 2000 and 2021, overall reimbursement for spine procedures (the backbone of private practice, forgive the pun) decreased 33% when adjusted for inflation with anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion taking the highest hit with a 39% decrease.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R5">5</a></sup></sup> As many of you know my wife Rachel is a health policy analyst and based on our dinner table conversations, this trend has if anything accelerated since 2021. Why did this happen? The answer is complex but it almost certainly has something to do with the fact that spending by the hospital lobbies and other special interests far outpaces anything organized medicine or organized neurosurgery can dream of spending. Physician payment represents only a small fraction of CMS expenses and neurosurgeons make up only a small fraction of physicians. We are not adequately represented by organized medicine and despite the herculean efforts of our Washington Committee, we have been largely on our own and have been largely outgunned.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-10">This decrease in reimbursement has occurred at the same time as a dramatic increase in practice expense related to continued pressure on liability coverage, salary expenses, and the real estate boom. Stark laws and other federal regulations have significantly limited the ability of physicians to participate in the ownership of health care facilities including hospitals, imaging facilities, and rehabilitation units. Finally, the Affordable Care Act and associated legislation such as the Hi-Tech act, have largely eliminated community hospitals as a meaningful source of employment for neurosurgeons. The unreimbursed expenses related to the adoption of electronic health records and the substantially increased reporting burdens made survival impossible for all except the largest of systems. As more and more community hospitals and small systems failed, the larger systems grew larger and larger with care now almost exclusively centralized in major centers. This situation was exacerbated by the COVID epidemic where many health systems were simply overwhelmed with desperately ill but poorly renumerated patients. Accompanying the coalescence of hospitals into mega-health systems, the associated administrative burdens led to the creation of a whole new population of middle men, the hospital administrators.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-11">The growth in hospital administrators has been staggering over the last several decades. A quick google search (November 24, 2025) revealed that the number of health care administrative positions grew 3800% from 1970 to 2019 with an accompanying increase in the number of physicians by 200%. In 2019, this resulted in a health care administrator to physician ratio of greater than 10:1. I went to the Bureau of Labor Statistics to try and back up this claim. Although I could not replicate the exact numbers reported by Google, most likely due to different inclusion criteria used by various authors, the 2025 data indicate that healthcare service manager positions continue to increase at an annual rate of 23%, that healthcare information technician positions are increasing at an annual rate of 15%, and that physician and surgeon positions are increasing at 3% per year.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R6 R7">6,7</a></sup></sup> The situation has clearly not improved.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-12">What this has resulted in is a bureaucracy dedicated to its own propagation at the expense of physician autonomy and patient care. As I referred to earlier, the people responsible for professional and strategic decision making in building a neurosurgery practice are not neurosurgeons and are not interested in how, why, or on whom we operate. A hospital administrator's job is to make money for the hospital system. Since administrators cannot create any income because they do not do any reimbursable work in health care, their focus is on managing resources to create a positive balance between income and expenses. Neurosurgeons bring in a lot of income to a hospital. In fact, neurosurgeons provide the highest contribution margin of any specialty.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R8">8</a></sup></sup> Therefore, administrators tend to love neurosurgeons. However, administrators also must manage expenses, and neurosurgeons are both well paid and in general (acknowledging that all generalizations are false) savvy in terms of knowing their worth. A senior neurosurgery group servicing a hospital is completely justified in demanding call stipends, substantial subsidies, and other accommodations. As we have seen in multiple academic as well as private programs, control over surgeon performance and behavior has been hotly contested and in many cases there has been a rift between the existing neurosurgical community and hospital administration.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-13">This has resulted in many hospital systems looking for new recruits to replace the difficult to control and inconveniently self-aware private groups. Enter our graduates. Our graduates have the longest training obligation of any medical specialty. In my role on the neurosurgery residency review committee, we have had multiple discussions regarding the length of training and whether it can be shortened. In my opinion, I don't see that happening. The breadth and depth of our specialty continue to increase year after year after year. There are many commonly performed procedures in spinal surgery, functional neurosurgery, endovascular neurosurgery, and skull base surgery that did not exist when I trained that our current graduates must be familiar with. Complicating the equation is the fact that our residents are of a different generation. Most resident applicants have taken at least one or several gap years and many have spent years in the laboratory or in unrelated fields before working their way back to neurosurgery residency. Our graduates are now generally in their mid-thirties to early forties, most have families, many have huge amounts of debt, and all feel that they are ready to make up for lost time.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-14">Therefore we have the perfect storm of hospital administrators seeking to increase their bottom line and maintain control of one of their most profitable service lines hiring naïve graduates into positions which are destined to result in failure. Many of these systems are offering positions with huge salaries and generous signing bonuses to entice graduates into taking positions as hospital employed physicians. These positions are often associated with unrealistically high work Relative Value Unit (RVU) expectations and the signing bonuses are often nothing more than thinly disguised predatory loans. Here's how it works: the graduating resident is offered a huge salary and sign on bonus with the expectation that they will provide a certain volume of work for a certain period of time. If the graduate fulfills those expectations, they keep the signing bonus and maintain their salary. If not, then they may have to pay back the signing bonus or commit to a longer service obligation at a reduced salary. The graduating resident has little to no experience in negotiating contracts or on the business side of medicine. As an example, I was recently a visiting professor in Jacksonville, Florida. After giving my presentation, I had the opportunity to chat with the residents about some cases they had prepared and also about broader issues. Knowing that I was going to be talking about socioeconomic issues, I asked the senior residents what they thought a reasonable RVU expectation was for a newly minted graduate. The range of responses was wide, from 12 000 to 24 000 RVUs per year. Although this productivity can be obtained by senior surgeons in developed practices, I would describe that RVU burden as punishing or even impossible for a junior surgeon entering practice.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-15">I am not picking on the Jacksonville program, I have seen my own graduating residents making the same assumptions and as a member of the board, I have seen remarkable examples of RVU driven practice as a consequence of poorly considered contracts. It is very hard to get neurosurgery residents interested in the business aspects of practice. At our program we have in the past been cited for not providing enough education in this realm. In response we have created a series of talks specifically dedicated to billing practices, practice management, and life questions such as “what kind of disability insurance do I need?” I can tell you with complete honesty that these conferences tend to be the most poorly attended and the most poorly attended to by those who do show up. Residents tend to be buried in their laptops, taking sign out on their phones, or snoozing during these presentations. This is not because the residents are lazy or bad people, it is just that the topics are excruciatingly boring for young adults of that age whose clearly stated primary interests are in neuro-anatomy, surgical techniques, and controversies in patient management.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-16">The result is a train wreck. You have a phenomenally technically trained surgeon who has already spent their signing bonus on either paying off loans or buying a house who now finds him/herself stuck in a world of perverse incentives. In this world, the patient stops being seen as another individual in pain but as an opportunity to bill RVUs. This loss of humanism leads to poor decision making. Poor decision-making leads to poor outcomes. Poor outcomes lead to examination of the graduate's practice by the hospital administration and by local peers. Recall that these local peers may well be those who were fired to hire the new graduate. Relationships may not be all that warm and cozy and these local peers may take the opportunity to publicize the poor decision-making through notification of local credentialling authorities, the state board, and the ABNS. It is important to remember that even without such red flags waving, the ABNS closely evaluates the graduate neurosurgeon's first 125 cases. Even without a letter or stated concern, when the directors see patterns of over-operating, the hair on the back of their neck stands up and every case is examined with an even higher degree of scrutiny.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-17">What happens then? Lives and careers are damaged. Patients suffer through unnecessary surgeries and the associated short- and long-term consequences. Surgeons suffer from delay or denial of certification. Loss of certification makes it virtually impossible to practice within the greater community of neurosurgery. Loss of certification usually results in loss of employment.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-18">What role do we, the community of neurosurgeons, have in addressing this increasingly commonly observed phenomenon? What are our choices? First, we could do nothing. It is not unfair to say that these surgeons have made their choices and therefore should live with the consequences. However, what are the consequences of this choice? There are both philosophical as well as practical consequences. Philosophically, we have abandoned the concept of humanism as it applies both to our patients as well as to our progeny. To quote Richard Cohen, a Levinas Scholar from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte:<ul id="-2" class="wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet">
          <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">“To be human is to care for other above oneself, to overcome the natural indifference and countercurrent of being in nonindifference and compassion toward the other…the first word addressed to man, “Adam,” is a moral command. Because the human self is embodied and hence enjoys the elements, to care for the other's enjoyment becomes a visceral concern of the self, its moral obligation. Concerned for the concerns of the other, to be for the other before being for oneself is one's true self- without external identity and without internal identity- the self rises to the height of its proper humanity, its proper dignity.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R1">1</a></sup></sup>”</li>
        </ul>
      </p>
      <p id="JCL-P-20">If neurosurgeons abandon our humanism, can we claim to be a profession? Can we even exist as a distinct entity? Switching to a practical perspective, as we all know there are wolves barking at our door. Anesthesiologists are lobbying to perform and are performing minimally invasive spinal fusions, pain physicians with no surgical training are implanting complex devices, radiologists are certifying themselves to perform neurovascular surgery. Without a cohesive identity, we lose the ability to define ourselves. Without the ability to define ourselves, we are subject to being defined by others. With repeated examples of poor behavior, our ability to police ourselves becomes suspect.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-21">No one outside of this audience cares about this issue at all. I cannot imagine that a hospital administrator would care one bit if high margin procedures currently in the purview of neurosurgery are performed by other less trained physicians as long as they are being performed. The government certainly does not care. We have direct experience of the systematic destruction of neurosurgical private practice through the actions of both parties. Making matters even worse, the government currently is threatening the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education and American Board of Medical Specialties over concerns of restriction of trade based on claims of unfair competition by rogue board certified practitioners with vague training histories and expansive claims of expertise. The public does not care- they do not know enough to be terrified of the dissolution of our specialty, and it is tough to generate sympathy for disaffected 1%-ers.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-22">So, if doing nothing is a poor option, what options do we have to preserve the culture and identity of neurosurgery? I am going to go out on a limb here and say that there is an option and that our community through organized neurosurgery, and particularly the Congress of Neurological Surgeons, can help ameliorate the crisis. I spoke earlier about the value of mentorship. I gave two examples of very brief interactions that greatly influenced my career. A mentor provides perspective and wisdom in small doses. I would charge this community with developing a mechanism to provide mentorship for our graduates during their first five years in practice. In addition to providing advice with what realistic expectations are in a particular job, a mentor can provide broader guidance—keep the patient as the focus (as Bob Dempsey did for me), forgive and remember your mistakes (Greg Trost and Peter Jannetta for me), get your boards taken care of early, and save your stupid life choices for later in life (me to every graduating resident). I was fortunate to develop in an environment rich with mentors, not all of our graduates have such a blessing. I would move that we create a mechanism to enable mentor/mentee relationships outside of the individual practice. Given the realities of the hospital employed model, local neurosurgeons may be hostile competitors. A mentor cannot be in direct competition, and they cannot be motivated by anything but the desire to help. I am stretching the usual concept of humanism as it applies to patients to apply to our progeny and asking for your help and the Congress's help in establishing a network of experienced neurosurgeons outside of the academic structure to function as mentors. This concept is something we discussed more than a decade ago when I was involved in the leadership of the Congress. At that time, there was not a huge interest. I think that now, given the evolution of the job market and the erosion of our specialty's sense of culture, may be the time. Thank you very much for your time and attention.</p></section><section id="article-references" class="article-references js-article-references"><h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL0">Acknowledgments</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-23">I have to acknowledge the influence that my training partners at the University of Pittsburgh had on me. These men and women are superbly talented and forced me to up my game to keep up. I must personally thank my chiefs, Greg Thompson and Mark Linskey for their patience and perseverance in dragging me along, my litter mates Gino Bonaroti and Jeff Campbell for putting up with me longer than anyone else, and my junior crew Alan Scarrow, Mel Fields, and Jim Burke for forgiving my attempts at teaching and leadership. I also must give a special shout out to Elad Levy, Brian Subach, and Mark McLaughlin for their immense entertainment value. Finally, Mike Groff was a student rotating with us during my junior year and we became very close and stayed close for the duration of his career. I miss him very much and wish he was here to listen to this talk. I need to thank my partners at the University of Wisconsin. Bob Dempsey has created a wonderful collegial environment that I and many others have prospered in. I have benefited from being surrounded by internationally known superstars as well as caring and compassionate physicians throughout my career. Greg, Mustafa, Benny, Than, Azam, David, Wendell and others; see <span><a href="https://www.neurosurgery.wisc.edu/people/" onclick="javascript:window.open('https://www.neurosurgery.wisc.edu/people/');return false">https://www.neurosurgery.wisc.edu/people/</a></span> for a full list of the Department of Neurological Surgery faculty and staff. Things have not always been smooth and certainly not always pretty. That said, I am blessed with five amazing children, Leah, Sabrina, Talia, Eli, and Zev who continue to amaze me with their own wisdom and compassion. I feel so blessed to have all of you in my life and am even more blessed by Isla, Addie, and Zoe- the next generation! Finally, thank you Rachel. Thank you for “undumping” me years ago and thank you so much for your uncompromising compassion and incredible support.</p>

      <li id="ej-article-indicators-free" class="ejp-article-indicators__list-item" onmouseover="javascript:Tooltip_Free()" onmouseout="javascript:Tooltip_MouseOut()"><span class="ejp-indicator">Free</span></li>
    </ul></section><div class="ejp-fulltext-content js-ejp-fulltext-content"><section id="ArticleBody"><h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL0">INTRODUCTION:</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-0">Glioblastoma (GBM), the most aggressive primary brain tumor, is notoriously resistant to treatment due to the protective blood–brain barrier (BBB), which limits chemotherapeutic penetration. Focused ultrasound (FUS) with microbubbles (MB) offers a noninvasive method to transiently disrupt the BBB, potentially enhancing drug delivery to infiltrative tumor regions.</p>
      <h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL1">METHODS:</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-1">This Phase I trial at Northwestern University enrolled adults (≥18) with recurrent GBM after 1–2 prior therapies. BBB disruption was achieved via SonoCloud-9, an implantable device with nine ultrasound emitters placed over the tumor bed. A total of 68 sonication cycles were performed with concurrent intravenous MB infusion and chemotherapy. BBB opening was assessed using gadolinium-enhanced MRI. Drug concentrations—carboplatin (CBDCA) and paclitaxel (PTX)—were measured in sonicated vs. non-sonicated brain tissue.</p>
      <h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL2">RESULTS:</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-2">LIPU/MB significantly enhanced intratumoral drug concentrations. CBDCA increased 9.3-fold (8.21 µM ±1.65 vs. 0.88 µM ±0.38). PTX rose 3.7-fold (0.1386 µM, 95% CI: 0.0828–0.2319 vs. 0.0373 µM, 95% CI: 0.0223–0.0625; p < 0.0001). The brain-to-plasma (B/P) ratio of PTX increased 3.6-fold (p = 0.00013), and that of CBDCA rose 5.8-fold (p = 0.0002). Absolute brain CBDCA concentration also increased 5.9-fold (p = 0.00012).</p>
      <h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL3">CONCLUSIONS:</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-3">LIPU/MB enables safe, reversible BBB disruption, markedly improving chemotherapeutic delivery in GBM. The procedure was well tolerated, with transient grade 1 headaches as the most common adverse effect. This approach may overcome BBB limitations and improve GBM and CNS therapy outcomes.</p></section><section class="ej-article-copyright">© Congress of Neurological Surgeons 2026.         if (!displaySubscriptionType) {
            displaySubscriptionType = subscriptionType;
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showthanksmessage') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = "block";
            mainPanel.style.display = "none";
            thankYouMessageAuthenticated.innerHTML = "Thank you for subscribing to the " + displaySubscriptionType + " for " + journalTitle + ".";
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showemail') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = "none";

      <div id="article-abstract-content1">
        <div class="ejp-article-text-abstract">
          <p>Single-cell chromatin accessibility analysis enables high-resolution dissection of regulatory elements and gene regulatory mechanisms. However, standardized and comprehensive analysis workflows remain limited. In this study, we present a streamlined pipeline for analyzing single-cell chromatin accessibility data. The workflow begins with data preprocessing using single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (scATAC)-pro or Cell Ranger ATAC, followed by peak calling with MACS2 and differential accessibility analysis to detect open chromatin regions and perform differential accessibility analysis to highlight regulatory differences among cell populations. Transcription factor activity is then inferred using chromVAR, incorporating motif enrichment and footprinting analysis. Finally, SCENIC+ is applied to reconstruct transcriptional regulatory networks, enabling in-depth exploration of epigenetic mechanisms at the single-cell level. This integrative approach offers a robust framework for decoding the regulatory landscape and understanding cellular heterogeneity in complex biological systems.</p>

      <div id="article-abstract-content3">
        <p><span class="ejp-indicator">Plain Language Summary</span>This study introduces a streamlined pipeline for analyzing single-cell chromatin accessibility data, which helps uncover regulatory elements and gene mechanisms. The process starts with data preprocessing using scATAC-pro or Cell Ranger ATAC, followed by peak calling with MACS2 to identify open chromatin regions. Differential accessibility analysis highlights regulatory differences among cell populations. Transcription factor activity is inferred using chromVAR, which includes motif enrichment and footprinting analysis. SCENIC+ is then used to reconstruct transcriptional regulatory networks. This comprehensive workflow provides a robust framework for exploring epigenetic mechanisms and cellular diversity in complex biological systems.</p>

    </div></section><div class="ejp-fulltext-content js-ejp-fulltext-content"><section id="ArticleBody"><h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL0">1. INTRODUCTION</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-3">Various approaches have been developed to study chromatin accessibility, such as deoxyribonuclease I hypersensitivity sequencing (DNase-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R1 R2 R3">1–3</a></sup></sup> formaldehyde-assisted isolation of regulatory elements (FAIRE-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R4">4</a></sup></sup> micrococcal nuclease digestion with sequencing (MNase-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R5">5</a></sup></sup><sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">,</sup><sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R6">6</a></sup></sup> assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing (ATAC-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R7">7</a></sup></sup> and nucleosome occupancy and methylome sequencing (NOMe-seq).<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R8">8</a></sup></sup> ATAC-seq is a method for mapping chromatin accessibility genome-wide using a hyperactive Tn5 transposase, which inserts sequencing adapters into accessible chromatin regions.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R9">9</a></sup></sup> ATAC-seq is faster, simpler, and requires fewer cells than DNase-seq and MNase-seq, which are more time-consuming and costly due to their large cell requirements and separate assays.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R7">7</a></sup></sup> However, bulk ATAC-seq is unable to determine chromatin accessibility at the single-cell level, thereby limiting its application in identifying cell subpopulations. To address these limitations, single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq) has been developed. Leveraging the advantages of the ATAC-seq protocol, scATAC-seq can measure chromatin accessibility on the single-cell level and the data richness of single-cell genomics has been substantially expanded.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R10">10</a></sup></sup> scATAC-seq data has become a popular tool for examining chromatin accessibility at the single-cell level. scATAC-seq has emerged as a powerful approach for dissecting cell type-specific regulatory programs, identifying rare cell populations, and inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs).</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-4">However, scATAC-seq data analysis poses unique computational challenges, necessitating robust pipelines for preprocessing, peak calling, differential accessibility analysis, motif enrichment, and regulatory network reconstruction.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-5">Current pipelines for scATAC-seq analysis offer a diverse toolkit, each with unique strengths and limitations. ArchR stands out for its scalability and rich visualization features, making it ideal for large datasets, though it can be memory-intensive and primarily R-based.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R11">11</a></sup></sup> Signac,<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R12">12</a></sup></sup> as part of the Seurat ecosystem, excels at multi-omic integration with scRNA-seq and offers flexibility, but may struggle with very large datasets and lacks some automation. SnapATAC<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R13">13</a></sup></sup> is highly efficient and fast, particularly well-suited for large-scale clustering, yet its bin-based approach can lead to lower resolution at the peak level. cisTopic<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R14">14</a></sup></sup> provides interpretable topic modeling for regulatory programs but may have limitations in scalability and integration with other data types. MAESTRO<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R15">15</a></sup></sup> is valuable for joint scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq analysis, but can be complex to configure. Meanwhile, Cell Ranger ATAC is user-friendly and standardized for 10x data, but lacks flexibility for non-10x platforms or advanced customization. scATAC-pro<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R16">16</a></sup></sup> is a comprehensive tool for processing, analyzing, and visualizing single-cell chromatin accessibility sequencing data. Overall, tool choice depends on specific goals such as integration, scale, or user expertise, and no single pipeline yet dominates across all criteria. The current protocol provides a pipeline for downstream bioinformatics analysis of scATAC-seq (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F1', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 1</a></strong>).</p><section class="ejp-r-article-images"><figure class="ejp-r-article-images__figure"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__image-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F1', '02118581-202603000-00013')"><img class="ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load" src="javascript:void(0);" data-src="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F1.jpeg" data-srcset="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F1.jpeg 2x" srcset="" alt="F1"></a><figcaption class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F1', '02118581-202603000-00013')">Figure 1.: </a><div class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text">Schematic workflow for single-cell ATAC-seq data processing and downstream analysis. The analysis pipeline begins with raw sequencing data (FASTQs) processed using Cell Ranger ATAC and scATAC-pro for alignment, demultiplexing, trimming, mapping, and filtering. ArchR is then used to create Arrow files and projects, followed by quality control and doublet filtering. Dimensionality reduction and clustering enable identification of cell populations. Downstream analyses include peak calling, identification of marker peaks and features, TF motif search, and TF footprint analysis. ATAC = assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, TF = transcription factor.</div></figcaption></figure></section><h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL1">2. PREPARATION</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-6">For data analysis, it is essential to have access to a computational server or a high-performance computing environment, since handling data at this scale can be too demanding for most regular computers. A fundamental understanding of command-line tools and bioinformatics is required for implementing the pipeline.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-7">Hardware requirements:</p>
      <ul id="JCL1-4" class="wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet">
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">High-performance computing server (minimum 64 GB RAM recommended).</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">Linux-based system (Ubuntu 20.04 or CentOS preferred).</li>
      </ul>
      <p id="JCL-P-10">Data requirements:</p>
      <ul id="JCL1-6" class="wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet">
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">Single-cell ATAC-seq raw sequencing reads in FASTQ format: 5k peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a Healthy Donor (Next GEM v1.1) (5k PBMCs from a Healthy Donor [Next GEM v1.1]—10x Genomics).</li>

Epi Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression dataset analyzed using Cell Ranger ARC 2.0.0 (PBMC from a Healthy Donor—Granulocytes Removed Through Cell Sorting [3k]—10x Genomics).</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">Genome reference (eg, human hg38, mouse mm10): Download the reference genome. Download the appropriate reference genome file from the 10x Genomics official website (<span><a href="https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/downloads/latest" onclick="javascript:window.open('https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/downloads/latest');return false">https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/downloads/latest</a></span>) based on the species studied.       </div><br><h2 class="ejp-article-outline-heading" data-level="1" id="JCL3">4. STEP-BY-STEP METHOD DETAILS</h2>
      <p id="JCL-P-15"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 1: Data preprocessing with Cell Ranger ATAC</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-16">Before analysis, ensure Cell Ranger ATAC is installed, the reference genome files are downloaded, and the sequencing-derived FASTQ files are prepared.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-17">Install Cell Ranger ATAC Refer to the official documentation(<span><a href="https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/pipelines/latest/installation" onclick="javascript:window.open('https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/pipelines/latest/installation');return false">https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/pipelines/latest/installation</a></span>) for installation.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-18">1.1 Create a working directory and extract data</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-19">>mkdir scATAC_analysis</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-20">>cd scATAC_analysis</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-21">1.2 Run Cell Ranger ATAC to generate single-nucleus accessibility counts</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-22">For the subsequent analysis in this tutorial, we will utilize the dataset titled <em xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">5k PBMCs from a Healthy Donor (Next GEM v1.1</em>) provided by 10x Genomics.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-23">> cellranger-atac count</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-24">--id=atac_pbmc_5k_analysis \</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-25">--reference=/path/to/reference/refdata-cellranger-arc-GRCh38-2020-A-2.0.0/ \</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-26">--fastqs=/path/to/fastq_files/atac_pbmc_5k_nextgem_fastqs \</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-27">--sample= atac_pbmc_5k_nextgem \</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-28">--localcores=8 \</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-29">--localmem=64</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-30">1.3 Check Output Files</p>
      <ul id="JCL3-11" class="wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet">
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">outs/summary.csv: Quality control statistics</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">outs/filtered_peak_bc_matrix.h5: Cell-by-peak matrix</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">outs/cloupe.cloupe: Visualization file for Loupe Browser</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">outs/fragments.tsv.gz: Input File Types in ArchR</li>
      </ul>
      <p id="JCL-P-35">Note: Cell Ranger ATAC is tightly integrated with the data format and platform of 10x Genomics single-cell ATAC-seq, making it potentially incompatible with data from other sources. Therefore, we introduce an alternative tool here: scATAC-pro.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-36"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 2: Data preprocessing with scATAC-Pro</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-37">scATAC-pro is an integrated open-source computational toolkit designed for processing, analyzing, and visualizing sequencing datasets from single-cell chromatin accessibility experiments.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R16">16</a></sup></sup> The scATAC-pro framework comprises 2 core functional units: a data processing unit and a downstream analysis unit. The data processing unit accepts raw FASTQ files as input and generates critical outputs, including a peak-by-cell count matrix, a quality control (QC) metrics report, and genome browser-compatible track files. This protocol focuses specifically on the data processing pipeline. Its workflow encompasses 7 key modules: sample demultiplexing, adapter sequence removal, read alignment to a reference genome, chromatin accessibility peak detection, cell barcode identification, genomic track file generation, and comprehensive quality assessment.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-38">2.1 scATAC-pro installation</p>
      <ul id="JCL3-16" class="wk-article__list wk-article__list--plain">
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--plain">- Compile from source code on GitHub.</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--plain">- Run using a pre-configured Docker image.</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--plain">- Install required dependencies (Python ≥3.7, R ≥4.0, Bowtie2, etc).</li>
      </ul>
      <p id="JCL-P-42">Execute the following command in your terminal to deploy scATAC-pro to the specified installation directory: YOUR_INSTALL_PATH/scATAC-pro_1.5.2</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-43">>git clone <span><a href="https://github.com/wbaopaul/scATAC-pro.git" onclick="javascript:window.open('https://github.com/wbaopaul/scATAC-pro.git');return false">https://github.com/wbaopaul/scATAC-pro.git</a></span></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-44">>cd scATAC-pro</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-45">>make configure prefix=YOUR_INSTALL_PATH</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-46">>make install</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-47">2.2 Input requirements</p>
      <ul id="JCL3-20" class="wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet">
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">FASTQ files for pair-end1 reads(pe1_fastq.gz), pair-end2 reads(pe2_fastq_gz) and cell barcords (index_fastq.gz)</li>
        <li class="wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet">for data generated by 10x, you can just specify the path to each FASTQ file folder per sample</li>
      </ul>
      <p id="JCL-P-50">2.3 Step-by-step guide to running scATAC-pro</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-51">Execute the scATAC-pro pipeline sequentially by configuring the PEAK_CALLER (eg, MACS2) and CELL_CALLER (eg, FILTER) parameters in the configure_user.txt file prior to runtime.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-52">>scATAC-pro -s demplx_fastq</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-53">-i pe1_fastq.gz,pe2_fastq.gz,index_fastq.gz</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-54">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-55"># or for 10x data</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-56">>scATAC-pro -s demplx_fastq</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-57">  -i pbmc_10x_fastqs/</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-58">  -c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-59">>scATAC-pro -s trimming</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-60">-i output/demplxed_fastq/pbmc5k.demplxed.PE1.fastq.gz,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-61">  output/demplxed_fastq/pbmc5k.demplxed.PE2.fastq.gz</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-62">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-63">>scATAC-pro -s mapping</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-64">-i output/trimmed_fastq/pbmc5k.trimmed.demplxed.PE1.fastq.gz,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-65">  output/trimmed_fastq/pbmc5k.trimmed.demplxed.PE2.fastq.gz,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-66">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-67">>scATAC-pro -s call_peak</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-68">-i output/mapping_result/pbmc5k.positionsort.MAPQ30.bam</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-69">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-70">>scATAC-pro -s aggr_signal</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-71">-i output/mapping_result/pbmc5k.positionsort.MAPQ30.bam</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-72">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-73">>scATAC-pro -s get_mtx -i output/summary/pbmc5k.fragments.tsv.gz,output/peaks/PEAK_CALLER/pbmc5k_features_BlacklistRemoved.bed</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-74">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-75">>scATAC-pro -s qc_per_barcode -i output/summary/pbmc5k.fragments.tsv.gz,output/peaks/PEAK_CALLER/pbmc5k_features_BlacklistRemoved.bed</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-76">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-77">>scATAC-pro -s call_cell</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-78">-i output/raw_matrix/PEAK_CALLER/matrix.mtx</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-79">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-80">>scATAC-pro -s get_bam4Cells</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-81">-i output/mapping_result/pbmc5k.positionsort.bam,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-82">output/filtered_matrix/PEAK_CALLER/CELL_CALLER/barcodes.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-83">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-84">Some of the processing modules can be run together by a single command:</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-85">In one mode, processing data including demplx_fastq, mapping, call_peak, get_mtx, aggr_signal, qc_per_barcode, call_cell, and get_bam4Cells.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-86">>scATAC-pro -s process</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-87">-i pe1.fastq.gz,pe2.fastq.gz,index.fastq.gz</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-88">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-89"># or for 10x data</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-90">>scATAC-pro -s process</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-91">  -i PATH_TO_10x_fastqs_directory</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-92">  -c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-93">In another mode, conduct all processing modules except demultiplexing step.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-94">>scATAC-pro -s process_no_dex</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-95">  -i pe1_fastq,pe2_fastq</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-96">  -c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-97"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 3: Analysis of single-cell chromatin accessibility data with ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-98">The first thing we do is change to our desired working directory, set the number of threads we would like to use, and load our gene and genome annotations. Then, using ArchR, we import the fragment files from the output of Cell Ranger ATAC to create ArrowFiles and an ArchRProject.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-99">3.1 Load ArchR</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-100">>library(ArchR)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-101">>library(parallel)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-102">>library(ggplot2)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-103">>inputFiles <- getTutorialData(“Hematopoiesis”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-104">>set.seed(123)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-105">>addArchRThreads(threads = 16)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-106"># We recommend setting threads to 1/2 to 3/4 of the total available cores.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-107">>addArchRGenome(“hg38”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-108"># addArchRGenome(“hg19”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-109">Note: ArchR has built-in support for “hg19,” “hg38,” “mm9,” and “mm10.” You can also use the createGeneAnnotation() and createGenomeAnnotation() functions to build your own genome and gene annotations.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-110">3.2 Create ArrowFiles</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-111">As a powerful tool for single-cell ATAC-seq data analysis, ArchR is compatible with diverse data input formats, with fragment and BAM files being the most commonly used. Subsequently, we employ the fragment files generated by the 10x Genomics Cell Ranger ATAC as input files in ArchR.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-112"># Locate Fragment Files</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-113">>inputFiles <- c(“Sample1” = “/path/to/atac_pbmc_5k_analysis/outs/fragments.tsv.gz”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-114"># Create Arrow Files</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-115">>ArrowFiles <- createArrowFiles(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-116"> inputFiles = inputFiles,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-117"> sampleNames = names(inputFiles),</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-118"> minTSS = 2,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-119"> # Dont set this too high because you can always increase later</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-120"> minFrags = 1000,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-121"> addTileMat = TRUE,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-122"> addGeneScoreMat = TRUE</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-123">)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-124">We can inspect the ArrowFiles object to see that it is actually just a character vector of Arrow file paths.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-125">3.3 Per-cell quality control</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-126">In ArchR, QC of scATAC-seq data is crucial for eliminating low-quality cells. This process focuses on 3 key aspects: the number of unique nuclear fragments, the signal-to-background ratio, and the fragment size distribution. In the prior step, we applied relaxed thresholds for the minimum transcription start site (minTSS) enrichment score and the minimum mapped ATAC-seq fragments per cell (minFrags). This allowed an initial evaluation of the data quality. For each sample, ArchR automatically generates a cell density heatmap of TSS enrichment score and number of ATAC-seq fragments. Arrow files creation produces a “QualityControl” folder in the current directory, containing 2 plots per sample. One plots log10(unique nuclear fragments) against TSS enrichment scores, with thresholds marked by dotted lines (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 2A</a></strong>). The other displays fragment size distributions (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 2B</a></strong>).</p><section class="ejp-r-article-images"><figure class="ejp-r-article-images__figure"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__image-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013')"><img class="ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load" src="javascript:void(0);" data-src="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F2.jpeg" data-srcset="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F2.jpeg 2x" srcset="" alt="F2"></a><figcaption class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013')">Figure 2.: </a><div class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text">Quality control and doublet detection of scATAC-seq data. (A–B) Quality control metrics of sample 1. (A) TSS enrichment score versus log<sub xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">10</sub>(unique nuclear fragments) per cell. Dotted lines represent filtering thresholds applied for downstream analysis. Cells passing these thresholds (n = 5278) exhibited a median of 14,877 fragments and a median TSS enrichment score of 20.64, indicating good data quality. Fragment size distribution (B) showing characteristic mono- and di-nucleosome peaks, supporting successful transposition and library construction. (C) Doublet identification plots. UMAP projection showing doublet enrichment scores (left), indicating the relative enrichment of simulated doublets compared to expectation. UMAP projection of doublet scores (middle), reflecting the statistical significance (−log<sub xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">10</sub> binomial-adjusted <em xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">p</em> value) of doublet enrichment for each cell. LSI = latent semantic indexing, scATAC = single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, TSS = transcription start site, UMAP = Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection.</div></figcaption></figure></section><p id="JCL-P-127">3.4 Doublet Inference with ArchR</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-128">Single-cell data from any platform is prone to doublets, where one droplet contains one barcoded bead and multiple nuclei. This makes reads from multiple cells appear as a single cell. It is especially problematic in developmental/trajectory data, as doublets can be mistaken for intermediate cell types or states. We can observe that the addition of doublet scores leads to the generation of 3 related plots: doublet enrichments (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 2C</a></strong>), doublet scores (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 2D</a></strong>), and doublet density (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 2E</a></strong>).</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-129">> doubScores <- addDoubletScores(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-130">input = ArrowFiles,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-131">k = 10,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-132">#Refers to how many cells near a “pseudo-doublet” to count.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-133">knnMethod = “UMAP,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-134">#Refers to the embedding to use for nearest neighbor search with doublet projection.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-135">LSIMethod = 1</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-136">)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-137">3.5 Create an ArchRProject</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-138">An ArchRProject serves as a centralized structure for integrating multiple Arrow files into a single, memory-efficient project. It enables rapid data access and manipulation, facilitating efficient interaction with Arrow files. As the foundation of most ArchR functions and analytical workflows, it streamlines data management and accelerates computational processes.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-139">>archr_proj <- ArchRProject(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-140"> ArrowFiles = ArrowFiles,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-141"> outputDirectory = “ output_ArchR,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-142"> copyArrows = TRUE</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-143"> # It keeps an original Arrow file copy for later use, as we’ll modify them downstream.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-144">)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-145">>getAvailableMatrices(archr_proj)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-146">Plotting sample fragment size distribution and TSS enrichment profiles.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-147"># Fragment size distributions</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-148">>p1 <- plotFragmentSizes(ArchRProj = archr_proj)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-149"># TSS enrichment profiles</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-150">>p2 <- plotTSSEnrichment(ArchRProj = archr_proj)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-151">>plotPDF(p1,p2, name = “QC-Sample-FragSizes-TSSProfile.pdf,” ArchRProj = archr_proj, addDOC = FALSE, width = 5, height = 5)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-152">We can save our archr_proj using saveArchRProject(), which will allow us to use this project in the future.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-153">> # save this project</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-154">>archr_proj <- saveArchRProject(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-155">  ArchRProj = archr_proj,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-156">  outputDirectory = “/Path_to_YourProject/archr_proj,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-157">  load = TRUE</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-158">  )</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-159"># load this project</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-160">>archr_proj <- loadArchRProject(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-161">path = “/Path_to_YourProject/archr_proj,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-162">force = FALSE</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-163">)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-164">3.6 Filtering doublets from an ArchRProject</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-165">A key part of this step is filterRatio, which is the maximum ratio of predicted doublets to filter, based on the number of pass—filter cells.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-166">>archr_proj1 <- filterDoublets(archr_proj)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-167">>archr_proj1 <- archr_proj1[which(archr_proj1$TSSEnrichment > 5 & archr_proj1$nFrags < 50000)]</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-168">3.7 Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) of dimensionality reduction</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-169">Dimensionality reduction in scATAC-seq is challenging due to the sparsity of the data, as most loci have zero accessible alleles, making traditional methods like PCA ineffective. To address this, latent semantic indexing (LSI),<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R23">23</a></sup></sup><sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">,</sup><sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R24">24</a></sup></sup> originally from natural language processing, is used. LSI normalizes data using term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and applies singular value decomposition (SVD) to reduce dimensionality while retaining important features. This transformation allows for effective visualization using UMAP or t-SNE, referred to as embeddings in ArchR.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-170">>archr_proj1 <- addIterativeLSI(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-171">ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-172">useMatrix = “TileMatrix,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-173">name = “IterativeLSI,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-174">iterations = 2,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-175">clusterParams = list(#See Seurat::FindClusters</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-176">  resolution = c(0.2),</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-177">  sampleCells = 5000,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-178">  n.start = 10),</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-179">varFeatures = 25000,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-180">dimsToUse = 1:30</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-181">)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-182">3.8 Clustering with ArchR</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-183"># Clustering using Seurat’s `FindClusters()` function</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-184">>archr_proj1 <- addClusters(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-185">  input = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-186">  reducedDims = “IterativeLSI”,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-187">  method = “Seurat”,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-188">  name = “Clusters”,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-189">  resolution = 0.05</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-190">)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-191">3.9 Single-cell embeddings</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-192">We use the addUMAP() function to run UMAP in ArchR and divide these cells into 5 clusters(<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 3A</a></strong>).</p><section class="ejp-r-article-images"><figure class="ejp-r-article-images__figure"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__image-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013')"><img class="ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load" src="javascript:void(0);" data-src="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F3.jpeg" data-srcset="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F3.jpeg 2x" srcset="" alt="F3"></a><figcaption class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013')">Figure 3.: </a><div class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text">Chromatin accessibility landscape and differential peak analysis across identified cell clusters. (A) UMAP embedding based on Iterative LSI showing 5 distinct clusters (C1–C5) identified from dataset. Each dot represents a single cell, colored by its cluster assignment. (B) Heatmap of top marker peaks across clusters (C1–C5), generated by markerHeatmap. Accessibility scores are <em xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Z</em> score normalized, highlighting cluster-specific chromatin signatures.
