ATAC = assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, FDR = false discovery rate, LSI = latent semantic indexing, MA = mean-average, UMAP = Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection.</div></figcaption></figure></section><p id="JCL-P-193">>archr_proj1 <- addUMAP(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-194"> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-195"> reducedDims = “IterativeLSI,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-196"> name = “UMAP,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-197"> nNeighbors = 30,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-198"> minDist = 0.5,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-199"> metric = “cosine”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-200">>archr_proj1@embeddings</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-201">>p3 <- plotEmbedding(archr_proj1, colorBy = “cellColData,” name = “Clusters,” embedding = “UMAP”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-202">3.10 Batch effect correction with Harmony</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-203">If there are subtle batch effects, you can add more LSI iterations and start with a lower initial clustering resolution. For strong batch effect differences, use ArchR’s Harmony tool for correction.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-204">>archr_proj1 <- addHarmony(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-205"> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-206"> reducedDims = “IterativeLSI,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-207"> name = “Harmony,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-208"> groupBy = “Sample”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-209">>archr_proj1 <- addClusters(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-210"> input = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-211"> reducedDims = “Harmony,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-212"> method = “Seurat,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-213"> name = “Harmony_Clusters,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-214"> maxClasters = 35,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-215"> resolution = 0.8)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-216">>archr_proj1 <- addUMAP(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-217"> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-218"> reducedDims = “Harmony,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-219"> name = “UMAPHarmony,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-220"> nNeighbors = 30,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-221"> minDist = 0.5,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-222"> metric = “cosine”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-223">Beyond our chosen approach, several popular batch correction and integration methods have been evaluated for scATAC-seq data, including LIGER,<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R25">25</a></sup></sup> Harmony,<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R26">26</a></sup></sup> RPCA,<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R27">27</a></sup></sup> BBKNN,<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R28">28</a></sup></sup> and scVI.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R29">29</a></sup></sup> These tools differ in their underlying assumptions and performance across various feature spaces such as peaks, genomic windows, or gene activity matrices. Notably, only a minority (~27%) of integration attempts across diverse mouse brain datasets yielded improvements over unintegrated data, emphasizing the importance of feature selection.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R30">30</a></sup></sup> LIGER showed robust batch correction across peak and window spaces, though sometimes introduced artificial substructures. Harmony retained more biological variation but exhibited occasional subtype overlaps. RPCA and BBKNN offered a balance between correction and signal retention in small-scale datasets, though with limited scalability.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-224">Overall, when integrating scATAC-seq datasets, careful selection of feature space and tool is essential, as current methods often struggle to simultaneously remove batch effects and preserve biological fidelity—particularly in high-dimensional contexts.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-225">3.11 Defining cluster identity</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-226">Through manual annotation, we defined the 5 clusters as 4 cell types.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-227">>markersGS <- getMarkerFeatures(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-228"> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-229"> useMatrix = “GeneScoreMatrix,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-230"> groupBy = “Clusters,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-231"> bias = c(“TSSEnrichment,” “log10(nFrags)”),</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-232"> testMethod = “wilcoxon”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-233">>markerList <- getMarkers(markersGS, cutOff = “FDR≤0.05 & Log2FC≥1.0”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-234">>markerGenes <- c(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-235"> “CD34,” #Early Progenitor</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-236"> ”GATA1,” #Erythroid</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-237"> ”CD79A,” “MS4A1,” “CD19,” #B-Cells</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-238"> “CD14,” “MPO,” #Monocytes</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-239"> ”CD3D,” “CD8A,”#TCells</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-240"> ”NCAM1” #NK)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-241">>p4 <- plotEmbedding(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-242"> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-243"> colorBy = “GeneScoreMatrix,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-244"> name = markerGenes,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-245"> embedding = “UMAP,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-246"> quantCut = c(0.01, 0.95),</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-247"> imputeWeights = NULL)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-248">>cluster_annotations <- c(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-249"> “C1” = “Monocyte,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-250"> ”C2” = “Monocyte,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-251"> “C3” = “B Cell,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-252"> ”C4” = “T Cell,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-253"> “C5” = “NK Cell”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-254">>current_clusters <- archr_proj1$Clusters</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-255">>archr_proj1$celltype <- cluster_annotations[as.character(current_clusters)]</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-256">>p5 <- plotEmbedding(archr_proj1, colorBy = “cellColData,” name = “celltype,” embedding = “UMAP”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-257"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 4: Calling peaks with ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-258">Before calling peaks in ArchR, you must first run addGroupCoverages(), as ArchR relies on these group coverage objects for peak calling.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-259"># Making Pseudo-bulk Replicates</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-260">> archr_proj <- addGroupCoverages(ArchRProj = archr_proj1, groupBy = “Clusters”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-261">Peak calling was performed using MACS2 via ArchR’s “addReproduciblePeakSet()” function, with the parameters “--nomodel --shift -100 --extsize 200 --qvalue 0.05.” This configuration is recommended for scATAC-seq data, as it accounts for Tn5 transposase insertion sites and avoids model mis-specification in sparse single-cell data. Although ArchR includes a built-in peak caller, MACS2 is preferred due to its improved sensitivity and reproducibility.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-262">To ensure the robustness of peak calling, we evaluated 3 representative MACS2 parameter sets that varied in “—qvalue” and “—extsize.” All configurations yielded the same number of final union peaks (65,015) after ArchR’s reproducibility filtering, with only 8 peaks overlapping ENCODE blacklist regions in each case (<0.01%). These results indicate that peak detection in our dataset is highly stable and minimally affected by small changes in parameterization.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-263">For successful integration of MACS2, ArchR locates the executable through the system PATH or pip installation. If not automatically detected, the user can specify the exact binary location via the “pathToMacs2” argument. We recommend verifying the MACS2 version being used to avoid conflicts in multi-environment setups.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-264"># pathToMacs2 <- findMacs2()</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-265">>pathToMacs2 <- normalizePath(“/usr/local/bin/macs2”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-266">>archr_proj2 <- addReproduciblePeakSet(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-267"> ArchRProj = archr_proj2,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-268"> groupBy = “Clusters,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-269"> pathToMacs2 = pathToMacs2,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-270"> peakMethod = “MACS2,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-271"> additionalParams = “--nomodel --shift -100 --extsize 200 --qvalue 0.05”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-272">>getPeakSet(archr_proj2)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-273"># Adding a Peak Matrix</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-274">>archr_proj3 <- addPeakMatrix(archr_proj2)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-275"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 5: Differential chromatin accessibility peaks analysis</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-276">In many cases, identifying peaks that are unique to a specific cluster or a small group of clusters is crucial. In ArchR, this can be achieved in an unsupervised manner by utilizing the addMarkerFeatures() function in combination with the useMatrix = “PeakMatrix” parameter. This approach allows for the detection of cluster-specific chromatin accessibility features, providing valuable insights into the distinct regulatory landscapes of individual clusters.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-277">>markersPeaks <- getMarkerFeatures(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-278"> ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-279"> useMatrix = “PeakMatrix,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-280"> groupBy = “Clusters,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-281"> bias = c(“TSSEnrichment,” “log10(nFrags)”),</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-282"> testMethod = “wilcoxon”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-283">>markerPeaksList <- getMarkers(markersPeaks,cutOff = “FDR≤0.05 & Log2FC≥1.0”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-284">ArchR provides multiple plotting functions that interface with objects returned by SummarizedExperiment, enabling visualization of marker peaks within the ArchR framework(<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 3B–D</a></strong>).</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-285"># Marker Peak Heatmaps</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-286">>heatmapPeaks <- markerHeatmap(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-287">  seMarker = markersPeaks,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-288">  cutOff = “FDR≤0.1 & Log2FC≥0.5,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-289">  transpose = TRUE)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-290">>draw(heatmapPeaks, heatmap_legend_side = “bot,” annotation_legend_side = “bot”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-291"># Marker Peak MA and Volcano Plots</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-292">>pma <- plotMarkers(seMarker = markersPeaks, name = “C4,” cutOff = “FDR≤0.1 & Log2FC≥1,” plotAs = “MA”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-293">>pv <- plotMarkers(seMarker = markersPeaks, name = “C4,” cutOff = “FDR≤0.1 & Log2FC≥1,” plotAs = “Volcano”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-294">>plotPDF(pma, pv, name = “Tcell-Markers-MA-Volcano.pdf,” width = 5, height = 5, ArchRProj = archr_proj3, addDOC = FALSE)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-295"># Marker Peaks in Browser Tracks</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-296"># C4--CD3D--T cell</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-297">>p6 <- plotBrowserTrack(</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-298">  ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-299">  groupBy = “Clusters,”</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-300">  geneSymbol = c(“CD3D”),</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-301">  0features = getMarkers(markersPeaks, cutOff = “FDR≤0.1 & Log2FC≥1,” returnGR = TRUE)[“C4”],</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-302">  upstream = 50000,</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-303">  downstream = 50000)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-304">>grid::grid.newpage()</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-305">>grid::grid.draw(p6$CD3D)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-306"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 6: Motif and feature enrichment analysis with ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-307">After identifying marker peaks, we can perform motif enrichment analysis on these peaks using the peakAnnoEnrichment() function. Marker peaks are typically derived from significantly differentially accessible peaks, identified through the getMarkerFeatures() function in ArchR. By using peakAnnoEnrichment(), we test whether these peaks are enriched for specific transcription factor (TF) binding motifs, helping to uncover potential TF regulatory relationships(<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 4A</a></strong>). This step provides critical insights into the gene regulatory mechanisms within different cell populations.</p><section class="ejp-r-article-images"><figure class="ejp-r-article-images__figure"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__image-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013')"><img class="ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load" src="javascript:void(0);" data-src="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F4.jpeg" data-srcset="https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F4.jpeg 2x" srcset="" alt="F4"></a><figcaption class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption"><a href="javascript:void(0)" class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link" onclick="showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013')">Figure 4.: </a><div class="ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text">TF motif enrichment and footprinting analysis across scATAC-seq-defined clusters.       <p id="JCL-P-317"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 7: ChromVAR deviations enrichment</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-318">ChromVAR is an R package designed to analyze sparse single-cell ATAC-seq data by quantifying variability in chromatin accessibility across peaks sharing the same motif or annotation while correcting for technical biases.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R20">20</a></sup></sup> In ArchR, this is achieved by first using chromVAR::getBackgroundPeaks() to define a set of matched background peaks, and then applying the addDeviationsMatrix() function to compute motif deviation scores for each cell across all annotated motifs. We can plot variable deviations (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 4B</a></strong>). This process generates a “MotifMatrix” that captures chromatin accessibility variation associated with TF binding. Through the names of the features we are interested in, we have plotted the distribution of chromVAR deviation scores for each cluster (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 4C</a></strong>).</p>

      <p id="JCL-P-354"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 8: TF motif annotation and footprinting analysis in ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-355">TF footprinting analysis predicts the precise binding sites of TFs on the chromatin, which typically requires high sequencing depth to achieve accurate results. To address this limitation, an integrative analytical strategy is implemented by systematically correlating predicted TF binding sites with the spatial distribution patterns of Tn5 transposase insertion sites. The accuracy of this footprinting analysis heavily depends on the availability of a reliable list of predicted binding sites for the TF of interest.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-356">Motif annotation in the ArchR workflow is performed using the addMotifAnnotations() function, which applies sequence matching algorithms to scan chromatin-accessible regions (peaks) for DNA sequences matching the target TF motifs. The results are stored in the ArchRProject object as binary annotations (0 = motif absent, 1 = motif present), indicating the presence or absence of the motif in each peak. While this approach efficiently identifies canonical motif elements, its accuracy can be limited by motif degeneracy, potentially overlooking non-canonical or low-affinity binding sites.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-357">Once motif annotations are generated, TF footprinting analysis is conducted using the getFootprints() function, which requires 2 inputs: the ArchRProject object and a set of motif coordinates in GenomicRanges format, derived from the getPositions() function. This procedure quantifies protection patterns at predicted TF binding sites, inferred from transposase (Tn5) insertion profiles, thus enabling the detection of TF occupancy at single-base resolution.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-358">This analysis framework is part of the validated ArchR pipeline, which provides scalable and efficient single-cell chromatin accessibility analysis, particularly suited for high-throughput scATAC-seq datasets.<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R11">11</a></sup></sup> The binary motif annotation structure, compatible with BSgenome, ensures computational efficiency for large-scale datasets and delivers structured inputs for downstream inference of GRNs.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-359">>motifPositions <- getPositions(archr_proj3)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-360">>motifs <- c(“GATA1,” “CEBPA,” “EBF1,” “IRF4,” “TBX21,” “PAX5”)</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-361">>markerMotifs <- unlist(lapply(motifs, function(x) grep(x, names(motifPositions), value = TRUE)))</p>

      <p id="JCL-P-367">The resulting footprints can be visualized using the plotFootprints() function, which displays the distribution of motif insertions, reflecting the binding activity of the TFs.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-368">To eliminate technical noise and reduce false-positive signals introduced by the sequence preference of Tn5 transposase, normalization for Tn5 bias is essential in footprinting analysis. This correction improves the specificity of footprint detection and ensures the reliability of downstream analyses. In this study, we applied 2 normalization strategies implemented in ArchR: subtracting Tn5 (<strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');">Fig. 4D</a></strong>) bias and dividing by Tn5 bias, each providing a distinct approach to account for bias-related artifacts in Tn5 insertion patterns.</p>

      <p id="JCL-P-393"><strong xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0">Step 9: Transcriptional regulatory network construction with SCENIC+</strong></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-394">Here, we employ SCENIC+, a comprehensive framework that integrates single-cell chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and TF motif information to reconstruct enhancer-driven gene regulatory networks (eGRNs).<sup xmlns:mrws="http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"><sup><a class="ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link" data-reference-links="R21">21</a></sup></sup></p>
      <p id="JCL-P-395">The resulting network allows high-resolution exploration of transcriptional regulation.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-396">While early steps of the chromatin accessibility analysis (eg, peak calling, clustering, and motif enrichment) were performed on an ATAC-only dataset, SCENIC+ analysis was conducted using a paired single-cell multiome dataset (RNA + ATAC) from 10x Genomics. This ensured compatibility with SCENIC+’s multi-modal regulatory network reconstruction framework.</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-397">9.1 Install SCENIC+ and Dependencies</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-398">Installing SCENIC+ in the new conda environment is highly recommended. It can be installed in a conda environment as follows:</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-399">>conda create --name scenicplus python=3.11 -y</p>

      <p id="JCL-P-402">>cd scenicplus</p>
      <p id="JCL-P-403">>pip install.</p>

    function alerts_ShowSubscribeeTOCPopup(journalTitle, journalId, subscriptionType, displaySubscriptionType) {
        $('#' + 'ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenSubscriptionType').val(subscriptionType);

        subscribeToEtocPopup.show();

        var modelPopupState = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenSubscribeToEtocPopupState');

        var thankYouMessageAuthenticated = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_lblAuthenticatedUserTitle');

        if (!displaySubscriptionType) {
            displaySubscriptionType = subscriptionType;
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showthanksmessage') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = "block";
            mainPanel.style.display = "none";
            thankYouMessageAuthenticated.innerHTML = "Thank you for subscribing to the " + displaySubscriptionType + " for " + journalTitle + ".";
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showemail') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = "none";
            mainPanel.style.display = "block";

            thankYouMessageUnAuthenticated.innerHTML = "Thank you for choosing to subscribe to the " + displaySubscriptionType + " for " + journalTitle + ".";
        }

        if ($('.etoc-popup') != null) {
            document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenJournalId').value = journalId;

            if (modelPopupState.value == 'showemail')
                emailTextBox.focus();
        }
    }

        <meta property="og:description" content="Breathing is a fundamental, innate behavior controlled by the neural circuits that integrate signals between the body and the brain. This process is precisely tuned to respond promptly to physiological stimuli, such as changes in blood gas levels and airway irritants, ensuring homeostasis and protecting the body from environmental challenges. Despite the vital importance, the mechanisms by which sensory signals are processed to regulate diverse breathing behaviors remain incompletely understood. In our recent research, we examined the molecular and functional diversity of neurons within the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) in mice, a critical relay center in the brain that receives afferent inputs from visceral organs. Using single-cell transcriptomics, we identified 19 molecularly distinct NTS neuronal populations, including two groups of neurons uniquely expressing neuropeptide genes. Through subsequent functional analysis, we discovered that optogenetic activation of these two NTS neuronal populations elicited distinct breathing behaviors: sighing and coughing, respectively. Further experiments, including chemogenetic inhibition and genetic ablation, demonstrated that these neuronal populations mediate specific respiratory responses to distinct interoceptive challenges. The first population was found to drive sighing behavior in response to hypoxia, while the second facilitated coughing during tussive challenges. We further identified two parallel neural circuits connecting the body and the brain, mediated by these neuronal populations, which process specific afferent inputs and engage distinct downstream pathways to regulate these breathing behaviors. Our work advances the understanding of the neural control of breathing by identifying endogenous circuits responsible for sighing and coughing. This research provides new insights into the organization of respiratory control circuits, with implications for understanding how the brain ensures robust breathing responses to physiological and environmental demands. data-core-wrapper="content"><div id="abstracts" data-extent="frontmatter"><div class="core-container"><section id="abstract" property="abstract" typeof="Text" role="doc-abstract"><h2 property="name">Abstract</h2><div role="paragraph">Breathing is a fundamental, innate behavior controlled by the neural circuits that integrate signals between the body and the brain. This process is precisely tuned to respond promptly to physiological stimuli, such as changes in blood gas levels and airway irritants, ensuring homeostasis and protecting the body from environmental challenges. Despite the vital importance, the mechanisms by which sensory signals are processed to regulate diverse breathing behaviors remain incompletely understood. In our recent research, we examined the molecular and functional diversity of neurons within the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) in mice, a critical relay center in the brain that receives afferent inputs from visceral organs. Using single-cell transcriptomics, we identified 19 molecularly distinct NTS neuronal populations, including two groups of neurons uniquely expressing neuropeptide genes. Through subsequent functional analysis, we discovered that optogenetic activation of these two NTS neuronal populations elicited distinct breathing behaviors: sighing and coughing, respectively. Further experiments, including chemogenetic inhibition and genetic ablation, demonstrated that these neuronal populations mediate specific respiratory responses to distinct interoceptive challenges. The first population was found to drive sighing behavior in response to hypoxia, while the second facilitated coughing during tussive challenges. We further identified two parallel neural circuits connecting the body and the brain, mediated by these neuronal populations, which process specific afferent inputs and engage distinct downstream pathways to regulate these breathing behaviors. Our work advances the understanding of the neural control of breathing by identifying endogenous circuits responsible for sighing and coughing. This research provides new insights into the organization of respiratory control circuits, with implications for understanding how the brain ensures robust breathing responses to physiological and environmental demands.</div><div role="paragraph">NIH R01AT011652, R01HL156989 (P.L.) and F31HL165733 (N.G.)</div><div data-type="disclaimer" role="paragraph"><b>This abstract was presented at the American Physiology Summit 2025 and is only available in HTML format.         <h1>Downloading to a citation manager</h1>

<p>This feature enables you to download the bibliographic information (also called citation data, header data, or metadata) for the articles on oursite.</p>

<h2>1. One or many?</h2>
<p>Download bibliographic data for one or several articles: The Download to Citation Manager feature is available on abstract and citation pages, as well as in search results. On a search result page use the check boxes to gather metadata for several articles at once.</p>

<h2>2. Citation manager file format</h2>
<p>Use the radio buttons to choose how to format the bibliographic data you're harvesting. Several citation manager formats are available, including EndNote and BibTex.<br></p>

<h2>3. Direct import</h2>
<p>If you have citation management software installed on your computer your Web browser should be able to import metadata directly into your reference database.</p>
<p><b><u>Checked</u></b>: When the Direct Import box is checked (the default state), a dialogue box will give you the option to Save or Open the downloaded citation data. Choosing Open will either launch your citation manager or give you a choice of applications with which to use the metadata. The Save option saves the file locally for later use.</p>
<p><b><u>Unchecked</u></b>: When the Direct Import box is unchecked, the metadata is displayed and may be copied and pasted as needed.</p>

                        <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 id="Abs1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number"> </span>Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>Current approaches to multimodal survival analysis based on pathology and genomics often apply attention mechanisms at a single stage, thereby missing fine-grained intra-modal details and cross-modal synergies. We propose a novel framework—<b>M</b>ultimodal <b>F</b>usion <b>F</b>ramework with <b>F</b>ull-stage <b>A</b>ttention (MFF-FA)—which integrates attention across three stages: feature extraction, modality alignment, and modality fusion. Specifically, we introduce En-UNI for pathology image sampling and representation, and employ attention modules to enhance latent genomic feature interactions. A convolution-based cross-attention module is further developed to model inter-modal correlations between pathology and genomics. Finally, a gating-attention fusion strategy is applied to retain modality-specific characteristics while enhancing their integration. Comparative evaluations demonstrate that MFF-FA outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in predictive accuracy for cancer survival analysis.</p></div></div></section>

                        <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 id="Abs1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number"> </span>Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>Integrating Artificial Intelligence of Every Medical Thing (AIoEMT) into personalized medicine represents a transformative shift toward individualized, data-driven healthcare. This research explores the AIoEMT framework's applications in optimizing diagnosis, treatment, and real-time therapeutic adjustments. By leveraging advanced AI techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, AIoEMT processes vast, heterogeneous datasets to uncover patterns that guide clinical decision-making. Key applications discussed include personalized cancer therapies, adaptive cardiovascular care, dynamic diabetes management, and AI-guided pharmacogenomics. The study also examines the role of data analytics in enhancing decision support systems, enabling proactive, evidence-based care. Furthermore, the research highlights data privacy challenges, algorithmic bias, and system interoperability, offering potential solutions such as federated learning and explainable AI. Real-time monitoring technologies, predictive models, and digital twin simulations demonstrate the potential of AIoEMT to predict disease trajectories and optimize treatments in dynamic environments. The findings underscore the transformative impact of AIoEMT on personalized medicine, enhancing treatment precision, patient outcomes, and healthcare system efficiency. As AI technologies continue to advance, AIoEMT is a critical enabler of precision medicine in the era of smart healthcare systems.</p></div></div></section>

                        <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 id="Abs1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number"> </span>Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>Gene expression could be perceived as a form of “cell language”, with underlying regulatory mechanisms akin to biological grammar. Decoding this language is critical in understanding cellular functions and behaviors. In this study, we proposed a new pre-training paradigm by integrating rich metadata and pre-training tasks, and developed scMulan, a multitask generative pre-trained language model for single-cell analyses. scMulan can accomplish multiple tasks in zero-shot manner such as cell-type annotation, batch integration, and conditional cell generation, guided by different task prompts. scMulan is also ready to be expanded for novel tasks through fine-tuning.</p></div></div></section><div class="c-article-section__content c-article-section__content--separator"><p>H.                         <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 id="Abs1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item">Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>Beyond traditional NLP applications, LLMs are now being applied to healthcare, biological modeling, and the biopharmaceutical industry, where their ability to maintain long context and understand complex relationships within datasets is proving immensely valuable. In a clinical context, LLMs are driving personalized medicine and medical education. By training on vast amounts of clinical data, these models can assist in identifying patterns and providing decision support, ultimately enhancing patient care. From clinical note generation to conversational agents for mental health, LLMs are reshaping how language-based interactions occur in healthcare and other critical fields. Their role in synthesizing and summarizing medical literature is also becoming indispensable for clinicians and researchers. Efficient extraction of insights from unstructured text (for instance, electronic health records) will become a significant part of daily clinical practice in the near future. In biological modeling, LLMs are being applied to DNA, RNA, and protein sequences, treating these biological molecules as a form of language. Models trained on genomic and proteomic datasets are uncovering intricate gene regulation patterns, predicting protein structures, and designing novel biomolecules, showcasing the potential of LLMs in computational biology. By integrating molecular, genomic, and clinical data, LLMs facilitate the identification of drug targets, prediction of molecular interactions, and accelerating drug discovery. This chapter explores the multifaceted applications of LLMs, with a focus on their impact in healthcare, biological modeling, and biopharmaceutical research. We will review the technical foundations of biological language models, the practical applications, and lessons learned in the development of such models. Finally, we will conclude the chapter by presenting topics that will be the focus of upcoming research in the field.</p></div></div></section>
